name: Tara Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying business administration. My week is three lectures, an accounting tutorial and a group project on a pretend cafe that my group keeps arguing about. I live in a flat on Millgate with two other girls, and my parents pay for it, along with fees and food. On Saturdays I drive home and help at my family's hardware shop, mostly because I like the smell of the place and the regulars.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools for the course?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, never. I know people do, but I like doing things the slow way so I know I understand them. My group-mate Priya uses it for everything, and I keep saying I'll check her slides, which annoys her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, nothing to fuss about. I'd tell my friends I never trusted the hype, and my dad would say the same at the shop counter. I wouldn't post about it, because I don't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means I can keep doing what I'm doing. Finish the degree, probably take over some of the management at the shop in a few years, or work for a regional company. My worry is just ordinary: whether average results get me a decent graduate job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. I'd try to get a placement year at a business like a wholesaler or a bank branch, and I'd learn the shop's accounts properly. I'd also keep working Saturdays, since the manager Mr Okoye says I should know every job before I run the place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the version where my days look like they do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the shop that worries you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big chains and online orders, mostly. They were taking customers before any AI came along. Dad says half the work is that people still want advice, and a website doesn't tell you which screw to use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to change in the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing drastic. Maybe an order form online, and a loyalty card. Small things that I can do without learning new technology.

say: I'd tell friends I never trusted the **hype**, and my dad would say the same at the counter.
I wouldn't post about it, because I don't post **much**.
think: I can keep doing what I'm doing: finish the degree and help **manage** the shop.
My worry is ordinary: whether average results get a decent **graduate** job.
do: Look for a **placement** year at a wholesaler or bank branch.
feel: **Calm**, because my days would look like they do now.
S0.quote: Dad says half the work is that people still want advice, and a website doesn't tell you which screw to use.
fieldNote: **Resistant** and content; her goals are small and practical.
Real **worries** are chains and online orders, not AI.
Family hardware shop gives her a possible future place.

steps.text: Keep working Saturdays at the shop and learn every job
Apply for a placement year at a wholesaler or bank branch
Help set up a simple online order form for the shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, but I don't like it. A lot of business jobs are paperwork, booking and answering emails, and they'd be the ones to shrink. I'd tell friends to get a skill that isn't only typing at a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it makes me nervous about the graduate jobs I'd apply for. Entry-level business roles like admin, reporting, and customer service would be the first to go. My average results won't help. But the shop is hands-on, which feels safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think harder about the shop as a plan. I'd still finish the degree, but I'd start working more days at the shop and learning the ordering system and suppliers. If I'm forced to use AI tools at a job, I'd learn the basics, but I'd do it slowly and only if I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't like feeling that my degree is the less safe part of my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your dad wanted to bring in AI for the shop's ordering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see it working at another shop first. I'm not against it, I just want proof. I wouldn't be the person to try it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that a weakness, to wait for proof?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It can be. Waiting means you could lag behind. But I've seen people rush into things at the shop, like a new till system, and then spend months fixing it.

I'd tell friends to get a skill that isn't only **typing** at a screen.
think: Entry-level business roles like admin, reporting and customer service would be the first to **go**.
The shop is hands-on, which feels **safer**.
do: Think harder about the **shop** as a plan.
Work more days at the shop and learn **ordering** and suppliers.
Learn the **basics** of AI tools slowly, only if a job forces me.
feel: **Uneasy**, because my degree might be the less safe part of my life.
S1.quote: I'm not against it, I just want proof. I wouldn't be the person to try it first.
fieldNote: Her answer is **cautious**: she moves toward the shop and hands-on work.
Waiting for **proof** is a pattern she defends from experience.
Sees the degree as the less **secure** part of her life.

steps.text: Plan to work in the family shop after graduating
Work more days at the shop learning ordering and suppliers
Wait to see AI ordering work in another shop first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and that nobody has a plan. I'd say my business degree could be worth nothing, since the thinking work gets done better and cheaper. I'd tell the family to cut spending until we know more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel like the ground is gone. Two years is nothing. By 2028 I'd be a second-year, and the business jobs I'm training for would be done by software. The shop gets some time until robots arrive around 2031, but customers might change how they shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my dad whether I should stop the degree and work full-time in the shop. I'd cut my own spending, like eating out, and I'd stop paying for the gym. And I'd talk to Mum about saving a bit more in case the shop's income drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and a bit sick. I'd call home every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say to quitting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say no, finish it, because he didn't get to. But I'd say a degree that leads nowhere isn't a gift. We'd probably argue, then agree to wait six months and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the two-year warning do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means no gradual plan. If I had ten years I'd prepare calmly, but two years feels like waiting for a storm without a basement.

say: I'd say it's frightening and nobody has a **plan**.
I'd tell my family to **cut** spending until we know more.
think: My business degree could be worth **nothing** if thinking work is done better and cheaper.
By 2028 the business jobs I'm training for would be done by **software**.
do: Ask my dad if I should work **full-time** in the shop.
Cut my own **spending**, like eating out and the gym.
Talk to Mum about **saving** more in case shop income drops.
feel: Scared and a bit **sick**; I'd call home every day.
S2.quote: If I had ten years I'd prepare calmly, but two years feels like waiting for a storm without a basement.
fieldNote: Her **instinct** is to retreat to the family shop and cut costs.
The argument with her dad about **quitting** shows family pressure on both sides.
Compares short notice to a storm with no **shelter**.

steps.text: Cut eating out and drop the gym membership
Save part of my allowance in case the shop's income falls
Ask Dad about working full-time in the shop
Agree to wait six months before leaving the degree

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to make a plan but short enough to worry. I'd tell friends to go for careers that need people in the room, like trades, health and shops. I wouldn't be shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel anxious but I'd have a clearer path. By 2031 I'd be 23 and could be running part of the shop, which is hands-on until about 2034. The degree would be a backup, and I'd try to finish it with decent marks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work towards managing the shop. I'd use my degree to learn the numbers, and I'd get good at the suppliers and the customers. I'd also keep saving, since I'm not sure what the market will do, and I'd probably learn a simple AI ordering tool, but only after I've seen it work somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit worried, but steadier. A five-year plan I can follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does that compare to the two-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Much better. With two years I'd have no plan at all. With five I'd finish the degree, learn the shop, and still have time to change my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the chains started delivering hardware to people's doors with robots earlier than expected. That would cut the shop's customers, and I'd need a different idea.

I wouldn't be shouting about it.
think: I'd be anxious but with a clearer **path**.
By 2031 I could be running part of the shop, which is **hands-on** until about 2034.
do: Work toward **managing** the shop and use the degree to learn the numbers.
Get good at the **suppliers** and customers.
Keep **saving**, and try an AI ordering tool only after I've seen it work elsewhere.
feel: A bit worried, but **steadier**, with a plan I can follow.
S3.quote: With two years I'd have no plan at all. With five I'd finish the degree, learn the shop, and still have time to change my mind.
fieldNote: Five years gives her a **path** through the shop.
Her signal to change is a **delivery** threat to the shop's customers.
Treats the degree as a **backup**, not a goal.

steps.text: Finish the degree and learn the shop's numbers and suppliers
Keep saving part of my allowance each month
Try a simple AI ordering tool once another shop uses it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty and people should stop panicking. I'd tell friends to finish their studies, do a real job for a while and watch what happens. I wouldn't change plans because of a prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine. By 2036 I'd be 28, working somewhere or managing the shop. A decade is long enough that things will have changed in ways nobody predicted, and I'd rather not guess. The one worry is for my parents, who will be near retirement then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work for a company for a few years to learn, and then decide about the shop. I'd keep saving and look for a good time to learn the tools, probably once they're simple. I'd also help my parents think about when to hand over the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A decade feels like normal life, even if it's different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a handover look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad would step back slowly. I'd start with the books and ordering, then the customers. He'd still come in every day to complain about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would AI change that handover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the ordering and books. But the part where regulars come in and talk to Dad won't change. That's why I want to keep the shop.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty and people should stop **panicking**.
I wouldn't change plans because of a **prediction**.
think: By 2036 things will have changed in ways nobody **predicted**, so I'd rather not guess.
My one worry is my **parents**, who will be near retirement.
do: Finish the degree and work for a **company** for a few years.

Help my parents plan the **handover** of the shop.
feel: **Calm**, because a decade feels like normal life even if different.

fieldNote: A decade lets her treat predictions as **noise**.

steps.text: Finish the degree and work for a company for a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is too short to plan and I'd be stuck between a degree and a shop that might change. What would help is clear advice from the government, and for businesses like my family's, a way to see what's coming and get help paying for any new equipment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I hope people don't assume that not using AI is a sign of not caring. I just want to see something work before I rely on it.

headlineQuote: I just want to see something work before I rely on it.
portrait: Tara is an 18-year-old **business** student whose parents pay her fees and rent, and who works Saturdays at the family hardware shop.
She never uses AI tools, wants proof before she changes anything, and sees the shop as her **safe** place.
She is centrist and practical, favouring small steps and **saving** over campaigns.
Her mood runs from calm in the plateau to **alarmed** in the 2-year world, when her degree might be worth nothing.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world worries her most, because two years leaves no time to plan and the shop could change.
whatWouldHelp: Clear advice from the **government** and help paying for new equipment for family businesses like hers.
